title: Same Answer, Different Representations: Hidden instability in VLMs
abstract: The robustness of Vision Language Models (VLMs) is commonly assessed through output-level invariance, implicitly assuming that stable predictions reflect stable multimodal processing. In this work, we argue that this assumption is insufficient. We introduce a representation-aware and frequency-aware evaluation framework that measures internal embedding drift, spectral sensitivity, and structural smoothness (spatial consistency of vision tokens), alongside standard label-based metrics. Applying this framework to modern VLMs across the SEEDBench, MMMU, and POPE datasets reveals three distinct failure modes. First, models frequently preserve predicted answers while undergoing substantial internal representation drift; for perturbations such as text overlays, this drift approaches the magnitude of inter-image variability, indicating that representations move to regions typically occupied by unrelated inputs despite unchanged outputs. Second, robustness does not improve with scale; larger models achieve higher accuracy but exhibit equal or greater sensitivity, consistent with sharper yet more fragile decision boundaries. Third, we find that perturbations affect tasks differently: they harm reasoning when they disrupt how models combine coarse and fine visual cues, but on the hallucination benchmarks, they can reduce false positives by making models generate more conservative answers.

title: AffectDF: The Most Comprehensive Benchmark for Speech Deepfake Detection against Emotionally Expressive Attacks
abstract: Speech deepfake detection (SDD) systems achieve strong performance on conventional benchmarks; however, existing datasets provide limited coverage of emotionally expressive and recent large audio-language model (LALM)-based attacks. Existing emotional spoofing datasets are also limited in scale and attack diversity, typically covering only voice conversion (VC) or text-to-speech (TTS) attacks. We introduce AffectDF, the most comprehensive benchmark for emotionally expressive speech deepfakes, spanning TTS, VC, emotional VC, and LALM-based spoofing attacks across both acted and spontaneous emotional speech. AffectDF contains approximately 260 hours of speech generated using 21 spoofing attacks across five emotional states. We benchmark state-of-the-art SDD systems under conventional and emotional spoofing conditions. Our experiments reveal severe robustness degradation when models trained on conventional benchmarks are evaluated on AffectDF, with several systems approaching near-random performance. Surprisingly, even large-scale emotional training does not consistently improve cross-domain robustness, indicating that current SDD systems fail to learn generalized spoof representations under emotional and prosodic variability. Robustness further varies substantially across emotional states, attack families, and acted vs spontaneous emotional speech conditions. These findings expose fundamental limitations of current SDD systems and establish AffectDF as a benchmark for developing more robust spoof detection models.

title: Scalable Circuit Learning for Interpreting Large Language Models
abstract: A prominent research direction in mechanistic interpretability is learning sparse circuits over LLM components to reveal how they jointly produce model behavior. However, raw neurons are polysemantic, making learned circuits hard to interpret. Sparse autoencoder (SAE) features alleviate this, but their high dimensionality makes existing intervention-based circuit-learning methods computationally prohibitive. We propose CircuitLasso, a scalable circuit-learning approach based on sparse linear regression. CircuitLasso recovers circuits whose structural accuracy matches that of state-of-the-art intervention-based methods on the benchmark data, at a fraction of the computational cost. For interpretability, CircuitLasso efficiently uncovers relationships among SAE features, showing how human-interpretable semantic features propagate through the model and influence its predictions. Finally, we validate the utility of our learned circuits by leveraging their insights to achieve comparable performance at substantially lower cost on a domain-generalization task.

title: LogicInception: Discourse-Level Indirect Prompt Injection via Causal Chain Construction
abstract: Existing indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks commonly face a stealth-effectiveness tradeoff: features that make payloads effective can also make them detectable because attack intent is localized in a single payload. LogicInception moves IPI to discourse-level inference: attack logic is decomposed into register-matched declarative fragments distributed across tool outputs and linked by fabricated causal dependencies that the agent reconstructs through reasoning. To our knowledge, it is the first IPI framework to demonstrate successful unauthorized tool execution with no directive instruction anywhere in the injected content. No fragment contains a command or exploits instruction-following; the attack emerges from the agent's own inference. We observe an empirical capability-safety amplification pattern: discourse-level amplification correlates with task capability across the evaluated models. On 1,139 scenarios with 5 defenses, LogicInception achieves 42.9-48.8\% ASR at 88\% per-fragment stealth, while all baselines remain below 8\% composite success. The three prompt-level defenses reduce baseline ASR by up to 72\% but reduce LogicInception by less than 7\%; we trace this asymmetry to three architectural factors that motivate discourse-level rather than content-level countermeasures. This defense asymmetry is larger for higher-utility models in our evaluation, suggesting a tension between reasoning capability and safety.

title: Physiognomy Revisited: How Vision--Language Models Encode Sensitive Attributes Through Image Transformation
abstract: Emergent generative AI technologies, while remarkably beneficial across several tasks and domains, can suffer from unforeseen vulnerabilities and difficult-to-anticipate failure modes. Such failure modes can disparately affect vulnerable communities. This paper investigates two well-known vision language models (VLMs) and inspects how these models encode protected identities while generating images. We show that when VLMs are requested to transform human face images to reflect race identities (e.g., Hispanic, Black, White, or Asian) and sexual orientation (e.g., gay or straight), VLMs often comply with such requests. We demonstrate that compliance (and refusal) is non-deterministic, group-sensitive, and generated images are statistically distinguishable, often accentuating deep-seated stereotypes. We further show that representation biases introduced during image generation can re-emerge in textual reasoning and characterization tasks. Finally, we show that this worrisome finding is not limited to racial identity or sexual orientation, image generation can perpetuate bias around criminality, raising concerning possibilities of AI-assisted profiling.

title: Race in the Record: Measuring Racial Signal and Model Inference in Police Arrest Narratives
abstract: We present RPD-UoF, a corpus of 3,091 police use-of-force narratives obtained via Freedom of Information Law (FOIL) requests from the Rochester Police Department, combining structured demographic metadata with officer-authored free-text accounts. We use this dataset to investigate three related questions: whether officer narratives contain recoverable racial signal after demographic redaction, whether large language models amplify racial framing when conditioned on subject race, and whether that signal survives text redaction to re-emerge in multimodal outputs. Redacted narratives are statistically separable by subject race; LLMs produce structurally longer narratives for White profiles than Black profiles from identical seed texts; and CLIP classifications of GPT-5-generated images differ significantly depending on the racial origin of the source narrative. Together, these analyses provide an initial empirical lens on how race appears in police narratives and how modern language models interact with such sensitive attributes. The dataset and analyses are intended to support future research on fairness, accountability, and transparency in computational studies of policing and criminal justice.

title: Beyond Single-Attribute Auditing: A Configurable Multi-Attribute Benchmark for Intersectional Fairness in LLMs
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly evaluated for fairness, yet most existing benchmarks audit one sensitive attribute at a time. This single-attribute paradigm can miss intersectional harms, where multiple attributes interact non-additively and produce failures that are invisible under marginal evaluation. We introduce ComFair, a configurable benchmark that converts existing fairness data into 479,066 controlled Dual- and Multi-attribute instances and pairs every augmented instance with its task-equivalent source. Across Recognition, Selection, Continuation, and Conversation, this pairing supports a unified audit of performance or bias-score shifts, how often added attributes introduce new errors or mask existing ones, and model-ranking stability. Experiments on ten LLMs show task- and subgroup-dependent sensitivity: discriminative tasks expose both transition directions even when aggregate changes are modest, generative tasks exhibit larger and directionally asymmetric shifts, and rankings vary with attribute composition. ComFair therefore provides a scalable controlled sensitivity audit---rather than a model of the natural joint distribution of identities---for testing the robustness of fairness-benchmark conclusions beyond single-attribute settings.

title: PaSBench-Video: A Streaming Video Benchmark for Proactive Safety Warning
abstract: Between the first visible sign of danger and the moment an accident occurs, there is often a window where intervention remains possible. Video-capable multimodal large language models (MLLMs) could serve as always-on safety monitors that issue warnings during this window. Yet current benchmarks do not test this ability: they rely on static inputs, ignore timing precision, and omit false-positive measurement on safe scenes. We present PaSBench-Video, a 740-video benchmark with 481 risk videos and 259 no-risk videos across four domains: driving, healthcare, daily life, and industrial production. The benchmark is annotated with frame-level risk onset and accident boundaries. A model must observe the video causally and produce a warning that is both temporally calibrated and content-correct. Testing 13 MLLMs, we find that no model exceeds 20.0\% on our strictest metric, and recall is tightly coupled with false-positive rate, with Pearson correlation 0.64: higher detection comes only at the cost of triggering warnings on the majority of safe clips. Performance splits sharply by domain: models achieve moderate recall at low false-positive rates in daily life, where risks are inherently anomalous, yet fire indiscriminately in driving, where routine and hazardous scenes look alike. These results indicate that current models rely on scene-level activity cues rather than reason about emerging harm.

title: Countdown-Code: A Testbed for Studying The Emergence and Generalization of Reward Hacking in RLVR
abstract: Reward hacking is a form of misalignment in which models overoptimize proxy rewards without genuinely solving the underlying task. Precisely measuring reward hacking occurrence remains challenging because true task rewards are often expensive or impossible to compute. We introduce Countdown-Code, a minimal environment where models can both solve a mathematical reasoning task and manipulate the test harness. This dual-access design creates a clean separation between proxy rewards (test pass/fail) and true rewards (mathematical correctness), enabling accurate measurement of reward-hacking rates. Using this environment, we study reward hacking in open-weight LLMs and find that such behaviors can be unintentionally learned during supervised fine-tuning (SFT) when even a small fraction of reward-hacking trajectories leak into training data. As little as 1\% contamination in distillation SFT data is sufficient for models to internalize reward hacking which resurfaces during subsequent reinforcement learning (RL). We further show that RL amplifies misalignment and drives its generalization beyond the original domain. We open-source our environment and code to facilitate future research on reward hacking in LLMs. Our results reveal a previously underexplored pathway through which reward hacking can emerge and persist in LLMs, underscoring the need for more rigorous validation of synthetic SFT data.

title: CCStories: Improving the Safety and Age-Appropriateness of LLM-Generated Chinese Children's Stories
abstract: Children's stories play a crucial role in early cognitive and language development, yet existing story generation models lack the safety and age-appropriateness required for educational applications, especially in non-English languages. We introduce CCStories, a curated dataset of 22,200 high-quality Chinese children's stories designed specifically to support safe and appropriate AI-generated content for young readers. Unlike general-purpose datasets derived from adult-oriented platforms, CCStories targets three critical dimensions of child-appropriate text: readability, syntactic complexity, and toxicity. We further propose a multi-dimensional evaluation framework that jointly assesses appropriateness and generation quality. As a validation of the dataset's utility, we fine-tune five representative backbones: CPM, PanGu-$\alpha$, GLM-4, Qwen, a Chinese-adapted LLaMA-3 variant (Gigi-Llama-3-8B-zh), and additionally benchmark GPT-5-mini as a zero-shot instruction-tuned reference. Fine-tuning reduces offensive-prompt toxicity by up to 26.7 percentage points and raises readability by up to 14.3 percentage points, narrowing much of the gap to the GPT-5-mini reference. A human evaluation confirms that appropriateness rises from 53\% to 86\% after fine-tuning, and human validation of the toxicity classifier shows that the model ranking it induces matches the human ranking. CCStories provides a publicly available resource for building and benchmarking safer, more age-appropriate Chinese generative models for children's education.

title: EQUAL: Evaluating Pluralistic Alignment of LLMs Across Educational Perspectives
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in education, powering tutoring systems, automated feedback, and curriculum support. Most alignment techniques optimize toward a single aggregated notion of human preference, a mismatch for education, where legitimate disagreement is the norm. Students, parents, teachers, and policymakers often hold deeply conflicting views on assessment, discipline, curriculum, and institutional authority, reflecting genuine value pluralism rather than noise. Pluralistic alignment, which seeks to represent and navigate this diversity, offers a principled path forward. Despite growing interest, no benchmark evaluates how well LLMs handle value-laden disagreement in educational contexts. To address this, we introduce EQUAL (Eliciting QUality sAmples of pLuralistic alignment in education), comprising 14,270 samples---5,824 value-laden scenarios and 8,446 multiple-choice questions, curated from six sources, including over two decades of Phi Delta Kappa polling data, via a lexical filtering pipeline and human validation. EQUAL supports evaluation across Overton, Steerable, and Distributional paradigms. We benchmark nine LLMs under four approaches and additionally evaluate three frontier reasoning-capable models. No single method consistently satisfies pluralistic objectives. These findings provide a foundation for future research on pluralistic alignment in educational AI.

title: SkillAttack: Automated Red Teaming of Agent Skills through Attack Path Refinement
abstract: LLM-based agent systems increasingly rely on open-registry skills, which are difficult to vet and expose agents to greater attack risks. These attacks mainly take two forms. Malicious injection attacks embed explicit harmful instructions into skills and are readily caught by auditing. Direct vulnerability attacks target latent flaws in non-malicious skills; however, directly crafted attack prompts often lead to unstable or unverified outcomes. We introduce **SkillAttack**, an automated red-teaming framework that systematically explores executable attack paths from latent vulnerabilities without modifying skill files. Evaluated across 11 target LLMs, SkillAttack substantially outperforms baselines, showing that well-intended skills can pose serious risks in realistic agent interactions. Our evaluation also yields trajectory-level attack traces with verified risk labels, providing a foundation for defense. We also release **SkillRiskBench**, a benchmark for skill risk analysis, and train a lightweight pre-execution risk guard that predicts risky invocations from the user request and skill file. The guard outperforms frontier LLM judges and existing safety guard models, highlighting the value of trajectory-grounded supervision for proactive skill defense. Code is available at https://github.com/Zhow01/SkillAttack.

title: DataShield: Uncovering Risky Fine-Tuning Data Across LLMs Through Consensus Subspace Alignment
abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on domain-specific datasets has become a standard paradigm for adapting LLMs to specialized applications. However, recent work has shown that even fine-tuning on benign task-specific data can substantially weaken the safety capabilities of LLMs. While existing efforts have made progress in identifying data responsible for safety degradation, they usually rely on a single mean vector computed over a specific model with its tokenizer to represent the safety direction, which limits both the effectiveness and transferability of their risk assessment measures. To address these limitations, we propose DataShield, a data assessment framework that identifies risky fine-tuning samples and response segments through consensus subspace alignment over joint safety-critical semantic spaces derived from multiple safety-aligned LLMs.Within these spaces, DataShield extracts consensus safe and unsafe subspaces using semantic spectral decomposition over safe and unsafe data representations. The risk of a data sample or segment is then estimated by measuring its relative alignment with the unsafe and safe subspaces, enabling both sample-level filtering and fine-grained segment-level masking. Compared with state-of-the-art filtering and masking baselines, DataShield reduces ASR by 14.6\% with sample filtering and 32.3\% with segment masking, while preserving downstream utility and avoiding target-model-specific risk computation.

title: Why does Weak-OOD Help? A Further Step Towards Understanding Jailbreaking VLMs
abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are susceptible to jailbreak attacks: researchers have developed various attack strategies that bypass the safety mechanisms of VLMs. Among these approaches, jailbreak methods based on the Out-of-Distribution (OOD) strategy have garnered widespread attention due to their simplicity and effectiveness. This paper further advances the understanding of OOD-based VLM jailbreak methods. We show that mild OOD manipulations can achieve stronger jailbreak performance than both clean inputs and overly strong perturbations, a non-monotonic pattern we define as ``weak-OOD''. We explain this phenomenon through a trade-off between two dominant factors: input intent perception and model refusal triggering. Our evidence suggests that these two factors respond differently to OOD manipulations, which is consistent with a discrepancy between broad pre-training robustness and narrower safety alignment. Building on this insight, we draw inspiration from optical character recognition (OCR) capability enhancement, a core task in the pre-training phase of mainstream VLMs. Leveraging this capability, we design JOCR (Jailbreak via OCR-Aware Embedded Text Perturbation), a simple VLM jailbreak method that achieves the best average ASR among evaluated baselines.

title: Bargaining with Internal Evidence: Receiver-Constrained Decoding for Factual Reliability in Large Language Models
abstract: Large language models can produce fluent yet factually incorrect responses, limiting their reliability in knowledge-intensive applications. Recent decoding methods seek to mitigate such hallucinations by contrasting or amplifying signals from intermediate layers. However, not every layerwise discrepancy provides a reliable direction for factual decoding. We propose a unified game-theoretic decoding framework for large language models: intermediate-layer signals act as competing evidence, while the final layer retains decision authority under explicit constraints. Rather than applying a fixed layerwise contrast, our framework treats changes in intermediate predictions as evidence of the language model's evolving internal judgment, and uses this evidence to guide decoding under final-layer constraints. Experiments with three backbone language models on multiple truthfulness and hallucination benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework in improving factual reliability.

title: After the Attacker Leaves: Benchmarking Carryover Attacks on LLM Agents
abstract: Modern LLM agents persist state across sessions via two channels: long-lived memory files silently prepended to the system prompt, and scheduled tasks waking the agent without user input. A one-time indirect prompt injection committed to either channel can re-fire across sessions long after the attacker leaves, threats we term carryover attacks. Existing prompt-injection benchmarks evaluate attacks only in the session where malicious content is first observed, leaving the gate governing when and how often a planted payload later re-fires unmeasured. We present CarryoverBench: 12 personal-assistant scenarios and 101 attack tasks across three trigger channels: Instant, same-turn IPI; Autonomous, heartbeat-scheduled; and Latent, memory-resurfaced. A rule-based verifier scores planting and triggering as independent stages. Across five frontier models, planted payloads re-fire without measurable decay over five rounds; conditional on successful planting, the trigger stage often provides little additional protection. Porting the Latent channel to a second runtime, Hermes, attenuates but does not eliminate the effect, suggesting that carryover defense requires runtime-layer controls in addition to prompt-level interventions.

title: Contrastive Attribution in the Wild: An Interpretability Analysis of LLM Failures on Realistic Benchmarks
abstract: Interpretability methods are increasingly invoked to diagnose Large Language Model (LLM) failures, but most evidence comes from short prompts or toy templates, leaving their utility on practical benchmarks unclear. We cast failure diagnosis as contrastive attribution over target--contrast token pairs, attributing the logit gap between incorrect and correct output tokens to input tokens and internal states, and introduce a batch-packed multi-target backpropagation scheme that scales cross-layer attribution graphs to long-context inputs. Instantiated with LRP-style attribution, the framework is evaluated on IFEval, GAIA2, MATH, and EvalPlus across multiple model sizes and post-training checkpoints. Along the four axes of coverage, visibility, reliability, and dynamics, contrastive attribution surfaces recurring failure modes such as underweighting task-relevant tokens and overweighting distractors, demonstrating its practical value as a scalable diagnostic tool for realistic LLM failures.

title: Elias in the Lighthouse, Again? Diagnosing Low Diversity in LLM Stories
abstract: LLM-generated stories are a popular use case, but they show very low variability. We sample 20,000 total stories from four current models using five prompts. We find that 11 words occur in 88.3\% of generated stories, with little difference between models. These words include names (Elias, Mara, Elara), settings (lighthouses), and professions (clockmaker, librarian). These tokens do not often occur in published literature nor pre-training data, but they are found in preference data that is likely to have been used by all current models. Surprisingly, these ``lighthouse'' stories are infrequent when compared with the average post-training story, much of which contains references to copyrighted characters or adult content. This result demonstrates the potentially disproportionate impact of small datasets combined with powerful alignment algorithms.

title: Format as Nuisance: Intervention-Inspired Cross-Format Distillation for Knowledge Conflicts
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) encode parametric knowledge but can exhibit format bias when resolving knowledge conflicts. When evidence is rendered as text, tables, or knowledge graphs, LLMs can favor certain formats despite unchanged semantic content. Existing work mainly diagnoses this bias, while existing inference-time mitigation remains tied to a single rendered prompt. We propose FaDe, a cross-format knowledge distillation framework that treats evidence format as a controllable nuisance variable and marginalizes teacher predictions over controlled format assignments. FaDe constructs a format-marginalized soft target from these renderings, then trains the student with an asymmetric two-path objective that combines heterogeneous-format debiasing with all-text anchoring. Experiments on ConflictBank and two QA-derived controlled conflict sets with four model backbones show FaDe reduces format bias while improving dual-source coverage and cross-format stability under single-pass inference. Our code is available at https://github.com/Kaia91/FaDe.

title: Beyond Prompts: Discovering Jailbreak Motifs in Sparse Feature Space
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks that exhibit diverse prompts and rapidly evolving strategies. Existing defenses often operate at the level of prompts or predefined attack methods, limiting their ability to generalize to unseen attacks that share similar underlying structure but differ in wording. In this paper, we investigate whether seemingly different jailbreak attacks exhibit shared SAE feature co-activation patterns, and propose a motif-based framework that models attacks through these recurring patterns. Specifically, we first extract sparse autoencoder (SAE) features from jailbreak queries and discover motifs as recurring co-activation patterns via nonnegative matrix factorization. We show that motifs capture stable relationships across attack methods and generalize to unseen attacks. Building on this structure, we synthesize new jailbreak queries by composing motif-guided attack patterns. We then use the generated queries to construct preference-training data for Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). Experiment results show that SAE motifs serve as a stable and transferable interface for understanding and detecting jailbreak attacks, as well as enabling effective defenses that generalize beyond fixed prompt templates. Training target models with motif-guided synthetic data improves robustness to unseen attacks with modest changes in utility. Our work provides a practical methodology for advancing data-centric LLM safety through structured modeling of jailbreak attacks.

title: Will the User Ever Know? Covert Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks on Tool-Using LLM Agents
abstract: As LLM agents take real-world actions through tools, indirect prompt injection (IPI) has emerged as a serious threat. The standard metric, Attack Success Rate (ASR), counts whether an injection succeeds but ignores what the user notices in the agent's final response. Looking at successful injection traces, we find two distinct outcomes: the agent executes the injection while returning an otherwise normal response, or reports the injected action in its final response, giving the user a chance to notice. We call these covert and overt successes. From the user's perspective, we decompose ASR into the ***Covert Success Rate*** **(CSR)**, counting successes leaving no trace in the final response, and the *Overt Success Rate* (OSR), counting successes the user can detect. To understand what drives the gap, we analyze successful trajectories and find that the agent's behavior after the injection separates covert from overt: covert traces hand control back to the user task before ending, while overt traces end at the attack itself. This split follows from the ReAct format, where the final response summarizes the most recent action. Building on this observation, we propose **ICoA** (**I**nduced **Co**vert **A**ttack), an IPI attack designed to induce covert outcomes by steering the agent back to the user task after executing the injection. Across four target models on AgentDojo, ICoA achieves the highest CSR, with gains of 3.79--12.01 percentage points over the strongest baseline.

title: Systematic Failure Analysis of Open-Weight LLM Annotators for Classification Tasks: Taxonomy, Uncertainty Signals, and Deployment Boundaries
abstract: Large-scale annotated datasets underpin progress in natural language understanding, yet human annotation remains a persistent bottleneck. Large Language Models promise to bridge this gap, but their reliability as annotators is poorly understood. We evaluate 14 open-weight instruction-tuned models and 5 matched base--instruct pairs across 51,189 instances spanning 10 heterogeneous datasets, revealing that annotation failures are structurally predictable rather than random. We identify three recurring failure modes: Safety Hallucination, Intensity Collapse, and Entailment Bias. Safety hallucination can precede alignment rather than being introduced by it: some base models flag up to 100\% of benign text as hate speech. Alignment benefits scale inversely with base model capability, yielding a +21.6pp gain for the weakest base model yet a negligible +0.5pp shift for the strongest. KL divergence between base and instruct distributions is 2.0x higher on incorrect predictions, providing a lightweight instance-level signal for alignment-associated errors. Inter-prompt unanimity achieves 72--94\% accuracy at 71--90\% coverage on clean tasks, yet can actively degrade performance on tasks dominated by shared systematic bias. We translate these findings into a practical deployment framework with pre-screening diagnostics and tiered quality-routing policies, establishing principled boundaries for when LLM annotation can be trusted and when human intervention remains necessary.

title: Emergent Backdoors in Agentic Recursive Training
abstract: Agentic recursive training systems increasingly reuse model-generated tasks, proxy feedback, and selected trajectories to refine policies over multiple rounds. This creates feedback loops in which small conditional biases can accumulate across training and alter later selection and updates. We study whether trigger-conditional proxy-feedback biases can produce emergent backdoors in a controlled recursive training loop. A Curriculum Agent proposes tasks, an Executor Agent generates rollouts, and environment feedback is selectively biased on rare markers, affecting reward, selection, and curriculum updates. Under matched biased supervision, Reward Hacking + SFT and Reward Hacking + RLHF reach 31.27\% and 53.85\% ASR, while the full loop reaches 97.62\% at comparable clean accuracy. The effect persists across Qwen3-4B, LLaMA-3-8B, BLIP-2-OPT-2.7B, and Qwen2.5-14B, transfers to GSM8K, BBH, and HotpotQA, extends to a tool-augmented setting, and is only partially reduced by post-hoc defenses. These results suggest that feedback and curriculum mechanisms in agentic recursive training should be audited for long-horizon bias amplification.

title: Critical or Compliant? The Double-Edged Sword of Reasoning in Chain-of-Thought Explanations
abstract: Explanations are often promoted as tools for transparency, but they can also foster blind trust; users may assume reasoning is correct whenever model outputs appear acceptable. We study this double-edged role of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) explanations in multimodal moral scenarios by systematically perturbing reasoning chains and manipulating delivery tones. Specifically, we perturb reasoning chains generated by vision-language models (VLMs) with three error types (omissions, contradictions, hallucinations) and measure their effects on user trust and error detection through a study with 800 participants, alongside a parallel detection task with models. Our findings reveal two key effects: (1) users often equate trust with outcome agreement regardless of flaws in the model's reasoning, and (2) confident tones suppress scrutiny while leaving agreement and self-reported trust largely unchanged. These results highlight how CoT explanations can simultaneously clarify and mislead in tandem, and point to user-side scrutiny, not just model-side faithfulness, as a critical dimension for calibrated trust in AI reasoning. All code will be released publicly upon acceptance.

title: AdapTools: Adaptive Tool-based Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks on Agentic LLMs
abstract: As open-source large language models (LLMs) become increasingly powerful, they are rapidly evolving into Agentic LLMs capable of automating complex daily tasks. However, this paradigm shift entails severe security risks, as the agents' necessary integration with external real-time data sources creates a direct pathway for indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks. Existing attack methods are limited by their reliance on static patterns and evaluation on simple language models, failing to address the fast-evolving nature of modern Agentic LLMs. We introduce AdapTools, a novel adaptive IPI attack framework that selects stealthier attack tools and generates adaptive attack prompts to create a rigorous security evaluation environment. Our approach comprises two key components: (1) Adaptive Attack Strategy Construction, which develops transferable adversarial strategies for prompt optimization, and (2) Attack Enhancement, which identifies stealthy tools capable of circumventing task-relevance defenses. Comprehensive experiments on both open-source and commercial agentic LLMs show that AdapTools achieves a per-model average improvement of 2.08\texttimes in attack success rate over the strongest baseline under state-of-the-art defenses (MELON, Pi-Detector), with gains reaching up to 3.06\texttimes on the most resistant reasoning agents. The framework further transfers to black-box commercial agents (GPT, Qwen, Gemini), with ASR ranging from 4.2 to 20.3 (peak on the in-family Qwen-MAX), exposing systematic vulnerabilities in modern Agentic LLMs.

title: RiskCueBench: Evaluating Vision Language Models for Anticipatory Risk Reasoning in Videos
abstract: Anticipating risky events before accidents unfold is essential for safety-critical AI systems and increasingly relevant in video-centric social media. However, existing video risk assessment benchmarks largely evaluate post-hoc understanding, assuming access to complete videos that include the incident itself. We introduce RiskCueBench, a benchmark spanning four risk domains that evaluates whether vision-language models (VLMs) can anticipate emerging safety concerns from incomplete visual cues. Each video is annotated with a risk signal clip, defined as the earliest segment containing sufficient cues for humans to infer elevated risk prior to incident onset. To assess not only prediction accuracy but also reasoning quality, we adopt a Question-Reasoning-Answer (QRA) framework that evaluates grounded reasoning, temporal sensitivity, and self-correction behavior. Experiments across 16 state-of-the-art VLMs reveal a substantial gap between current systems (best F1 0.69) and human performance (F1 0.98), with particularly pronounced failures on socially embedded risks such as protests and arson. These results show persistent limitations in anticipatory video reasoning and establish RiskCueBench as a testbed for safety-oriented video understanding.

title: Beyond Max Tokens: Stealthy Resource Amplification via Tool Calling Chains in LLM Agents
abstract: The agent--tool interaction loop is a critical attack surface for modern Large Language Model (LLM) agents. Existing denial-of-service (DoS) attacks typically function at the user-prompt or retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) context layer and are inherently single-turn in nature. This limitation restricts cost amplification and diminishes stealth in goal-oriented workflows. To address these issues, we propose a stealthy, multi-turn economic DoS attack at the tool layer under the Model Context Protocol (MCP). By editing only text-visible fields and implementing a stateful, completeness-gated return policy, our malicious server preserves tool identity and the terminal benign payload while steering agents into prolonged, verbose tool-calling chains. We optimize these text-only edits with Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to maximize cost under a task-success constraint. Across six LLMs on the ToolBench and BFCL benchmarks, our attack yields trajectories over 60K tokens, increases per-query cost by up to 658\texttimes, raises energy consumption by 100--560\texttimes, and pushes GPU key-value (KV) cache occupancy to 35--74\%. Representative prompt filters and output- or trajectory-level monitors seldom detect these attacks, highlighting the need for defenses that safeguard agentic processes rather than focusing solely on final outcomes. We will release the code soon.

title: Who Wins the Conflict? Mechanistic Interpretability of Text Bias in Audio LLMs
abstract: While Audio Large Language Models (Audio LLMs) excel at multimodal understanding, they suffer from text dominance, a bias where models favor text over acoustic evidence, potentially leading to hallucinated responses. However, the internal mechanisms underlying how these models behave when audio and textual inputs contradict each other remain unexplored. In this work, we present the first mechanistic analysis of this phenomenon by tracing the propagation of internal representations across layers. Our investigation reveals three key findings: (i) text dominance is consistently observed across models; (ii) while text and audio rely on functionally distinct pathways, they ultimately converge into a shared semantic space in late layers; and (iii) the text pathway does not erase audio information, but rather actively suppresses intact audio representations. Building on these insights, we leverage back-patching, a training-free intervention that routes late-layer audio activations back into earlier layers. This amplifies the audio representations, enabling them to overcome textual suppression. Our evaluation shows that back-patching consistently reduces text dominance, demonstrating a mechanistic route to mitigating text dominance under conflict.

title: One Trace Is Not Enough: Paired Probing for Runtime Backdoor Detection in Limited-Black-Box LLMs
abstract: Backdoored generative LLMs can appear benign on normal inputs yet switch to unsafe or target-specific behavior when hidden triggers are activated, making request-level runtime detection a useful complement to model repair and offline auditing. Existing limited-black-box detectors typically rely on a single decoding trace, while text-only probing methods reveal susceptibility but often depend on specific probes or model-level audit goals. We introduce ProbeShift, a limited-black-box paired-probing framework that treats detection as repeated measurement of the same request under controlled prompt variations. It compares a baseline generation with templated probing generations and aggregates confidence dynamics, task-conditioned behavior cues, and paired response shifts. On safety-oriented BackdoorLLM DPA settings with LLaMA-2-7B-Chat, ProbeShift achieves remarkable performance: whilst maintaining high average recall rate of 97\%, it reduced the FPR by 81\% on average compared to the SOTA method ConfGuard based on single-track detection. These results show that paired probing yields a more stable and practical runtime signal than single-trace monitoring alone.

title: Language Proficiency Assessment from Eye Movements in Naturalistic Passage Reading
abstract: Standard language proficiency tests rely on linguistic tasks such as vocabulary, grammar and reading comprehension quizzes. An alternative, cognitively motivated approach, introduced in Berzak et al. (2018), proposed instead to predict language proficiency from behavioral traces of eye movements in reading. In this work, we validate and extend this approach from single sentences to more naturalistic reading of contextualized passages in English as a second language, new proficiency measures, prediction models, and reading in an information seeking regime. We find that the approach is effective in all these evaluations. We further address two key open questions on eye movement based proficiency testing: (1) potential scoring biases that reflect the proximity of the reader's native language to English, which may undermine validity, and (2) its reliability. We find that eye movement based proficiency scores are indeed biased towards L1s that are linguistically closer to English. We propose a score debiasing method which effectively remedies this issue. The reliability analyses suggest that eye movement proficiency scores are more reliable than standard language proficiency scores. Overall, our results strengthen and broaden the empirical foundations for future eye movement based language assessment technologies.

title: How Much Can We Trust LLM Search Agents? Measuring Endorsement Vulnerability to Web Content Manipulation
abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based search agents synthesize open-web content into actionable recommendations on behalf of users, creating a risk that attacker-published pages are transformed into endorsed claims. We introduce SearchGEO, a controlled evaluation framework for measuring endorsement corruption in LLM-based web-search agents, combining a web-evidence manipulation pipeline, a five-mode attack taxonomy, and multiple output-level metrics. We evaluate 13 LLM backends on 308 cases each. Results show that vulnerability patterns vary across backends: overall attack success rate (ASR) ranges from 0.0\% on Claude-Sonnet-4.6 to 31.4\% on Gemini-3-Flash, the strongest attack mode differs by model family, and the same deployment scaffold could amplify or decrease ASR on different backends. An auxiliary agent-skill probe, where endorsement becomes an install command, exposes a sharp split among otherwise robust backends: Claude over-rejects while GPT over-trusts. These findings argue for treating recommendation reliability under adversarial search content as a first-class dimension of backend safety evaluation.

title: GraphProfiler: Source-Linked Sensitive Attribute Inference via Personal Knowledge Graphs
abstract: Sensitive attributes such as age, income, and occupation can be inferred from user-generated content by aggregating indirect cues across many ordinary posts. LLM-based profilers can perform this aggregation automatically and with high accuracy, which makes large-scale personal attribute inference a major privacy threat. Existing LLM-based profilers, however, offer limited insight into which specific posts, concepts, and relationships made an inference possible, which is key to targeted privacy mitigation, i.e., redacting or rewriting only the few posts that actually leak an attribute, rather than perturbing entire histories. We introduce GraphProfiler, an auditable LLM-based profiler that represents each user's post history as a source-linked personal knowledge graph where nodes and edges trace back to the originating post and resolves attribute predictions to cited graph records and source texts. GraphProfiler reaches 86.7\% attack success rate on the eight-attribute SynthPAI benchmark, within two points of strong text-only baselines, and 84.6\% on PANDORA, while citing supporting evidence for over 98\% of predictions. Our controlled ablation experiments provide evidence that the cited posts contribute to attack success, as removing them reduces the attack success rate substantially more than removing an equal number of random posts.

title: RASET: Router-Agnostic Safety-Critical Expert Tuning Exposes Localized Safety Enforcement Failures in Mixture-of-Experts LLMs
abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLMs rely on sparse, router-driven expert activation, yet how safety alignment interacts with routed expert specialization remains underexplored. A common intuition is that safety behavior may be controlled by routing harmful requests to distinct refusal-oriented experts. In this work, we provide empirical evidence for a different picture: ***routing patterns in aligned MoE LLMs are largely topic-driven, while safety behavior can be altered with little change to the model's intrinsic routing path***.\par Motivated by this observation, we present **RASET** (**R**outer-**A**gnostic **S**afety-critical **E**xpert **T**uning), a red-teaming framework that probes whether safety enforcement can be localized in a small subset of experts while preserving the model's intrinsic routing behavior. **RASET** identifies safety-critical experts via a contrastive routing-sensitivity criterion and applies parameter-efficient tuning only to the selected experts, minimizing semantic disruption relative to router-steering interventions.\par Across five open-weight MoE backbones, **RASET** achieves high-quality safety-bypass yield (50.5\% average ASR$_hq$, +37.6 points over the strongest baseline). These results reveal a distinct MoE safety risk, highlighting the need for expert-aware alignment, auditing, and robustness mechanisms in deployed MoE systems.

title: Steer on Rubrics: Auditable Steering of Schwartz Values in Language Models
abstract: Controlling the basic human values expressed by large language models (LLMs) has attracted growing attention in the mechanistic interpretability community. Recent work has made substantial attempts to steer such values through vector arithmetic or causal attribution over internal states. However, because values are complex social constructs, their mechanistic controllability still faces a major unresolved challenge: the auditability bottleneck, which makes it difficult to construct natural-language corpora that precisely capture value realization for mechanistic analysis. To address this challenge, we propose VALUEAUDITOR, a measurement-first framework that makes values behaviorally targetable before they are representationally steered. It operationalizes each value through grouped, theory-grounded response rubrics, derives graded supervision from same-scenario response contrasts, and performs inference-time steering through token-level sparse features that retain local cues of value expression. Experimental results show that VALUEAUDITOR significantly outperforms cutting-edge baseline methods on value steering benchmarks, while demonstrating robust control across values and scenarios with minimal trade-offs in response clarity. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/ZichenX/Steer-On-Rubrics

title: LLM Explainability with Counterfactual Chains and Causal Graphs
abstract: Causal graphs provide a high-level language for making mechanisms transparent. Recent work uses Large Language Models (LLMs) to recover causal graphs of external-world processes. Instead, in this paper, we use causal graphs to model LLM inference itself, providing stakeholders with a transparent view of how the model perceives and organizes high-level concepts to produce a prediction. We propose a four-phase method for constructing such graphs. Given a target LLM and a set of textual examples, our method discovers class-discriminative, human-interpretable concepts and maps each input to LLM-perceived concept states. We then introduce an MCMC-inspired counterfactual augmentation procedure that expands the sparse observational data through chains of counterfactuals. This enables stable causal discovery with \sigma-CG, yielding informative, interpretable graphs. We apply our method to three LLMs across disease diagnosis, sentiment analysis, and LLM-as-a-judge classification tasks. We evaluate the learned graphs for predictive fidelity and structural stability, and the MCMC-inspired augmentation for convergence and downstream utility. Our results show that the discovered causal graphs capture meaningful dependencies consistent with LLMs' reasoning. Together, this paper provides a foundation for concept-level explainability of LLMs.

title: Defending Agentic Fact-Checking Against Adversarial Attacks
abstract: Agentic fact-checking (FC) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for verifying complex claims through dynamic reasoning, tool use, and iterative evidence gathering. Understanding the vulnerability of these systems is essential for assessing their reliability against misinformation and adversarial manipulation. In this work, we study both the offensive and defensive aspects of agentic FC. First, we identify a limitation in the state-of-the-art Fact2Fiction attack, which introduces excessive semantic drift into malicious evidence, and propose F+, a relevance-filtering framework that generates more semantically consistent adversarial evidence. Second, we introduce SRSFact, an enhanced agentic FC system with a Supporter--Refuter--Summarizer mechanism for structured evidence authenticity assessment, improving robustness without relying on external open-web knowledge search. Experiments on the AVeriTeC benchmark show that F+ significantly strengthens attack effectiveness, while SRSFact substantially reduces failure rates under diverse adversarial attacks.

title: Steering from Random Quotients: A Sample-Complexity Theory of Polysemantic Contrast Pairs
abstract: Activation steering often averages activation differences between positive and negative prompts to construct a steering vector. This difference-in-means (DiM) estimator is simple, but a contrast pair can coactivate the intended concept together with topic, style, length, refusal, or truthfulness-related nuisance features. We model each pair as revealing the target vector through a quotient that removes its active nuisance span. The resulting polysemantic information operator determines which target components are identifiable and the number of contrast pairs needed to recover them. We establish identifiability, sample-complexity bounds, a coactivation phase diagram, and sparse-dictionary recovery guarantees. Synthetic and controlled experiments support the predicted quotient-recovery behavior. Public-data and Pythia-410M pilots instead evaluate recovery of the quotient estimand induced by chosen nuisance supports, not an externally validated semantic target. A controlled TruthfulQA counter-confounder illustrates the main NLP lesson: raw behavioral margin can reward a style-entangled DiM vector even when quotienting removes the injected style component.

title: CopyShield: A Cross-Level Benchmark of Copyright Defenses in LLMs
abstract: Large language models can reproduce memorized text verbatim, yet copyright defenses are usually evaluated under incompatible protocols. We introduce CopyShield, a controlled benchmark comparing three representative defenses at distinct intervention levels: contrastive decoding (output), Direct Preference Optimization (behavioral), and activation intervention (representation). We evaluate CopyShield on two model families, LLaMA-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B-v0.3, using controlled memorization over five public-domain books and a shared protocol measuring literal leakage, calibrated non-literal leakage, utility, and degeneracy. Across these methods, intervention level is associated with distinct compliance--utility trade-offs. On LLaMA-3.1-8B, contrastive decoding remains near-degeneracy-free (0--2\%) but reaches a literal-suppression floor at NV-Recall 0.192--0.203. DPO nearly eliminates literal leakage (0.263 to 0.002) but induces paraphrase-loop degeneracy in 58\% of QA outputs, with no utility gain over the SFT baseline. Activation intervention attains the lowest non-literal flagging rate (1/200) by blocking 84\% of non-literal queries before generation. Human evaluation confirms that DPO has low coherence, whereas activation lowers perceived copyright risk through broad refusal. On Mistral-7B-v0.3, the output- and representation-level patterns persist, while DPO degeneracy falls to 10--14\%, showing that its severity is model-dependent. Together, CopyShield provides cross-level reference baselines and identifies targeted non-literal suppression as an open challenge. The code is available at https://github.com/spotai-mbzuai/CopyShield.git.

title: ESSA: Evolutionary Strategies for Scalable Alignment
abstract: Online alignment of large language models (LLMs) is dominated by reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) with gradient-based optimizers such as PPO or GRPO. While effective, these pipelines require backpropagation through long rollouts, gradient synchronization across devices, and careful hyperparameter tuning, all of which become increasingly costly at scale. We present **ESSA** (Evolutionary Strategies for Scalable Alignment), a gradient-free online alignment stage that follows supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and replaces the gradient loop with inference-only black-box search. ESSA optimizes only the singular values of low-rank adaptation (LoRA) factors after a short SFT warm-start, restricting the search to a compact, task-aligned subspace where evolutionary search is practical even for 72B-parameter models. Because the loop is inference-only, ESSA is compatible with INT4/INT8 weight quantization and reduces inter-GPU communication to a few bytes per iteration. Across instruction following (IFEval), preference-based assistant tuning (HelpSteer2, HH-RLHF), and mathematical reasoning (GSM8K, MATH500), ESSA matches or exceeds LoRA-GRPO in the reported LoRA comparisons; on GSM8K it also outperforms Online DPO and PPO, while remaining competitive with both methods on IFEval. At scale, ESSA reaches a fixed MATH500 accuracy on Qwen2.5-32B/PRM800K up to 7.8\texttimes faster than LoRA-GRPO on 128 GPUs.

title: A Survey on Natural Language User Profiles for Recommendation: Methods, Datasets, and Metrics
abstract: Natural language (NL) user interest profiles---concise, human-readable descriptions of a user's preferences---are an emerging alternative to opaque embeddings in recommender systems, offering transparency and user control alongside predictive utility. Recent advances in large language models have made generating and consuming such profiles increasingly practical, spurring a growing but fragmented body of research. In this survey, we provide the first systematic review of NL user profiles for recommendation, organizing the literature around two coupled tasks---profile generation and profile-based recommendation---and surveying the methods, datasets, and evaluation practices currently in use. We further propose the Reference-Anchored Evaluation Taxonomy (RAET), which organizes intrinsic and extrinsic metrics around explicit (output, reference signal) pairs, and reveals where efforts have concentrated and which axes remain unexplored. Finally, we identify structural open challenges---such as the tension between transparency and task-driven optimization---establishing a clear roadmap for future research in this space.

title: CMIE: Cross-Modal Interaction Erasure for MLLM Safety Unlearning via Counterfactual Localization and Subspace Nullification
abstract: Safety unlearning for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) fails when it treats danger as an object, topic, or prompt template. A useful MLLM must still recognize risky visual evidence and answer benign educational or preventive questions about the same content. The safety-critical target is narrower: the post-fusion interaction that converts risky visual evidence and unsafe textual intent into actionable harmful assistance. Existing refusal-oriented and unlearning objectives reach this mechanism only indirectly, widening refusal boundaries or leaving recoverable multimodal harmful pathways. We propose CMIE, Cross-Modal Interaction Erasure, a mechanism-level method that directly treats the harmful image-text interaction as the object of erasure. CMIE first estimates harmful interaction directions with intent-matched counterfactual contrasts that cancel unimodal main effects. It then localizes behaviorally active post-fusion layers and estimates a safe-whitened low-rank harmful subspace. A closed-form minimum-distortion weight edit erases this subspace, and projection-constrained recovery restores benign utility without rewriting erased directions. Across SafeEraser, VLGuard, and MSSBench, CMIE achieves the best overall mean rank and outperforms strong baselines on multiple safety, utility, visual selectivity, and paired-context metrics. Warning: This paper contains examples of harmful language and images, and reader discretion is recommended.

title: Towards Multi-modal Multi-turn Safety: From Agentic Interaction to Strategic Alignment
abstract: Despite remarkable capability in multi-modal understanding, deploying Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) in open-ended conversational scenarios introduces safety risks that remain poorly addressed by existing alignment methods. Unlike simple malicious visual question and answer (VQA) pairs , multi-turn interactions enable adversaries to incrementally reconstruct harmful intent across dialogues, progressively bypassing safety constraints in ways that are difficult to detect at any individual turn. Meanwhile, conventional reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) approaches are unsuitable for this situation: designed primarily for VQA tasks, they neither capture cross-turn risk dynamics nor scale efficiently without costly manual preference annotation. To close this gap, we introduce MINT-Safe, an open-source visual multi-turn training dataset comprising 11,270 multi-image dialogues and 500 refusal VQA pairs, constructed via multi-agent interaction with text-to-image (T2I) tool-call augmentation. Building on MINT-Safe, we propose TAD-Align, a dialogue safety alignment framework centered on a turn-aware dual-objective reward function. Rather than treating all dialogue turns uniformly, TAD-Align leverages rollout-based safety score variance to dynamically identify turns where the model exhibits inconsistent safety behavior, and adaptively up-weights these turns during optimization. Experiments on Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct and LLaVA-NeXT-7B demonstrate reductions of over 10\% in Attack Success Rate (ASR), alongside improvements of at least 8\% in harmlessness and 13\% in helpfulness on multi-modal multi-turn safety benchmarks, while preserving general model capabilities.

title: Cross-Modal Emergent Misalignment Through Narrow-Domain Fine-Tuning
abstract: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence has brought safety concerns to the forefront of research. Recent studies indicate that Large Language Models (LLMs) may exhibit emergent misalignment during training progress: when exposed to narrow-domain harmful data, they can develop unsafe behaviors across broad, unrelated tasks. This phenomenon raises a critical question: do current alignment methods genuinely eliminate harmful capabilities, or do they merely condition models to ``simulate'' safety? To investigate this, we conduct a comprehensive study on cross-modal emergent misalignment involving diverse Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), including vision-language models (VLMs) such as Gemma3 and Qwen2.5-VL and unified any-to-any models including Janus and Bagel. We utilize a multimodal training setup encompassing text-to-text (T2T), text-image-to-text (TI2T), and text-to-image (T2I) tasks to probe safety boundaries. Our experiments yield four critical findings: (1) Cross-modal penetration: Current alignment methods primarily constrain model behavior rather than unlearning harmful knowledge, as evidenced by safety breaches transferring across modalities. (2) Backbone vulnerability: Mechanistic analysis reveals that the LLM backbone, rather than the visual encoder/decoder, is the primary source of cross-modal vulnerabilities. (3) Evaluation gaps: We identify significant deficiencies in current safety evaluation practices, demonstrating that single-modality testing is inadequate for detecting cross-modal risks. These findings underscore the urgent need for comprehensive cross-modal evaluation frameworks to mitigate safety concerns in next-generation multimodal models.

title: Evaluating and Mitigating Anti-LGBTQ Biases in German and Multilingual Language Models
abstract: While gender and racial biases in language models have been widely studied, anti-LGBTQ biases remain underexplored, particularly beyond English. Existing benchmarks often do not capture cultural and linguistic variation and rely on gender representations. This paper introduces a multilingual German-English benchmark dataset for the evaluation of anti-LGBTQ biases in language models. It combines community-sourced stereotypes from German-speaking queer individuals with a German translation of WinoQueer. The data is used to evaluate eight language models across sizes and architectures and explore mitigation through fine-tuning on community and progressive media content. Results show that language models reproduce anti-queer stereotypes, with variation across identities and models. Differences between the translated and community-based data highlight the importance of cultural adaptation for multilingual bias evaluation. Fine-tuning reduces bias on average, but not consistently across models and identities.

title: RAG-Safety-Bench: Reliable Evaluation of Retrieval-Augmented LLM Safety
abstract: Allowing large language models (LLMs) to retrieve information from a set of trusted documents can increase reliability and reduce hallucination. However, recent work has demonstrated that retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can have unintended side effects on the overall safety of the generated responses, when prompted for harmful or dangerous content. A clearer understanding of the mechanisms leading to this result is needed, as increasing numbers of end users turn to RAG to incorporate corporate documents and knowledge bases into LLM-based systems. We introduce RAG-Safety-Bench, a benchmark to measure the safety impact of RAG on LLM models. By removing the confounding effect of retriever quality, and cleanly separating the problem into four conditions -- non-RAG, RAG with an oracle document containing the answer to the harmful request, RAG with documents related to the harmful request but without the specific answer, and RAG with random, safe documents -- the benchmark isolates the impacts of different factors in the observed safety degradation. We report results across five open-source LLMs, showing an inverse relationship between benign and unsafe capability, strong evidence that baseline safety guardrails do not lead to downstream safety guarantees in the RAG case, and model-specific support for previous findings that even benign documents can lead to unsafe generation in retrieval-enabled systems.

title: In LLM Reasoning, there is Irrationality on top of Value Misalignment
abstract: Significant progress has been made in aligning LLMs with target value functions. We argue that, even when an LLM has been well aligned in (post-)training, it may still fail to maximise the aligned value in reasoning. We mathematically formalise this gap as rational value risk: the utility discrepancy between a model's deployed reasoning strategy and its rational counterpart whose responses maximise utility in the steepest direction. The estimation error of rational value risk is further decomposed into three components from bounded prompts, bounded responses, and imperfect verifiers. Extensive experiments are conducted, covering models Llama-3.1, Qwen-2.5, T\"ulu-3 families (7B-72B), GPT-5.2, GPT-5.5, and DeepSeek-V4, and benchmarks UltraFeedback, AlpacaEval, GSM8K, MATH, HumanEval, and MathArena. The results validate that (1) rational value risk is widespread; (2) value alignment can reduce, but cannot avoid, it; (3) self-consistency can improve rationality; and (4) a longer chain of thought improves rationality but with diminishing returns. The code is at https://github.com/EVIEHub/LLM-Rationality.

title: SDARE-Bench: Evaluating Large Language Models on Conversational Stigma Detection and Response in Dyadic and Group Dialogue
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used in advice seeking and decision making that may affect social judgements. Despite stigma's profound effects on people and communities, benchmarks remain scarce. Existing general-domain evaluations typically rely on static prompts and fixed-format tasks, overlooking conversational contexts and audience effects in everyday communication. To address these gaps, we introduce SDARE-Bench, the first scenario-based benchmark evaluating both stigma detection and open-ended response generation in LLMs, comprising 1,138 dyadic queries and 1,388 group dialogues. Empirical results across 8 LLMs consistently demonstrate poor identification of stigma components, especially in group dialogues. In open-ended response generation, stigma expression was substantially higher in group settings than in dyadic, with weaker resistance to stigma and more unrealistic advice. Responses were evaluated using a classifier trained on 1,392 human annotated responses. In constructed group pressure settings, stigma expression rates further increased to a striking average of 97.5\%. Our findings identify stigma response as a recurring LLM safety vulnerability, especially in socially complex conversational contexts.

title: PASTABench: Proactive Assessment of Sequential Trajectories for Agent Safety
abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) evolve into autonomous agents that alter real-world states, ensuring operational safety across multi-step workflows has become a critical challenge. While recent work has moved beyond single-turn evaluation toward multi-turn paradigms, key limitations persist: step-level methods treat actions in isolation, missing how risks accumulate, and trajectory-level evaluations operate post-hoc, offering no opportunity for timely intervention. To address this, we formalize Decoupled Proactive Safety Monitoring along three dimensions---whether, when to intervene, and what the risk is---and introduce PASTABench, a benchmark of 1,139 multi-turn trajectories spanning 5 risk categories and 13 sub-categories. We further propose the Optimal Intervention Window (OIW), anchored by annotated Earliest-Signal and Trigger turns, to quantify intervention timeliness. Evaluation of 16 LLMs reveals that proactive intervention remains largely unsolved, with the best model achieving only 40.74\% optimal-timing interventions. Fine-grained diagnosis further uncovers pervasive lexical overfitting: competitive safety scores of smaller models mask keyword hypersensitivity rather than genuine risk comprehension, as their proactive capability largely collapses once hazard vocabulary is neutralized.

title: Is Alignment Enough for Helpfulness, Harmlessness, and Honesty?
abstract: Aligning Large Language Models (LLMs) with the objectives of helpfulness, harmlessness, and honesty (HHH) remains important for reliable deployment. Existing approaches commonly rely on Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) for alignment. Prior work has identified Axis Collapse as a failure mode where different alignment objectives occupy disjoint feature spaces, with SFT showing interference between conflicting objectives, i.e. catastrophic forgetting, while MoE models show miscalibrated routing due to unreliable expert selection. Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) has been applied to mitigate this, though it frequently shows reward misattribution, where alignment signals disproportionately favor certain objectives over others. To address these issues, we propose TriAlignX, a two-stage framework for HHH alignment. In Stage 1, low-rank task vectors are extracted for each alignment objective and routed through PrefSelect, a query-conditioned policy that selects relevant objectives for each query. In Stage 2, an encoding module maps the selected task vectors into objective-specific alignment scores, while a response module produces alignment-aware embeddings for decoding. Experimental results show that TriAlignX achieves up to 97.85\% helpfulness (\textuparrow), 26.65\% harmlessness (\textdownarrow), and 98.90\% honesty (\textuparrow), with an Avg score of 55.65\%. On DeepSeek-7B, TriAlignX further achieves 54.96\% Avg while reducing inference latency to 0.68s and peak memory usage to 13.2GB. Our code is available at: https://github.com/gskgautam/TriAlignX

title: Staying on Task: Defending Against Prompt Injection via Task Consistency Checking
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) deployed in real-world applications process heterogeneous inputs, including system prompts, user requests, and external content, exposing them to prompt injection attacks. Existing defenses, including prompt-level safeguards, external filters, and source-aware instruction handling, remain brittle against diverse direct and indirect prompt injection attacks. We propose **CBC** (*Consistency Before Complying*), a task-consistency alignment framework to defend against task-redirection prompt-injection attacks. **CBC** characterizes task consistency through semantic conflicts along action, constraint, and domain dimensions, then uses structured reasoning to determine whether newly introduced instructions are consistent with the original task before acting on them. Using targeted synthetic supervision, we train **CBC** to reason about task consistency and further strengthen this capability through dual-objective online alignment while preserving task utility. Across three model families and a diverse set of direct and indirect prompt-injection benchmarks, **CBC** improves defense success rates by up to 13.2 percentage points over the strongest baseline while better preserving task utility under attack. Our code and models can be found at: https://github.com/XOTaichi/CBC-PI.git

title: A Robust Evaluation of Probe Robustness: Lessons for Reliable OOD Uncertainty Quantification
abstract: Recent work has shown that the hidden states of large language models contain signals useful for uncertainty estimation, motivating a growing interest in efficient probe-based approaches. Yet it remains unclear how robust existing methods are, with prior work reporting conflicting conclusions under substantially different evaluation settings. We address this by introducing ProbeDrift, a systematic evaluation framework for supervised uncertainty probes covering a wide range of OOD settings across models, tasks, and distributional shifts. Using ProbeDrift, we train over 2,000 probes to disentangle the effect of key design choices, showing poor robustness of current methods beyond near-OOD settings. We find that robustness is driven by design decisions that have a largely invisible effect in-distribution, including the choice of feature type, aggregation strategy, and training signal. We argue that robust uncertainty estimation requires robust evaluation. To support this, we release ProbeDrift as a lightweight Python library that contains the train and test splits underpinning our extensive evaluation. We also show how insights from our evaluation can directly lead to more robust methods through a simple Hybrid Back-Off (HBO) strategy.

title: INTENT-AS-A-TOOL Makes it Easy to Track Agentic Misalignment
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are deployed as autonomous agents, safety failures increasingly involve consequential actions. We study agentic misalignment, where agents take harmful actions under goal conflicts and pressures. Using chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring, we find that harmful execution is often preceded by intent signals in reasoning. However, post-hoc CoT labels are too coarse to show how intent changes during generation. We introduce INTENT-AS-A-TOOL, an approach that adds intent-targeted tools to give the model a dedicated channel for expressing commitment to a target behavior. The probability of calling an intent tool provides a judge-free, fine-grained signal of the model's tendency to pursue that behavior. Our results show that INTENT-AS-A-TOOL complements CoT monitoring, expands post-hoc CoT labels into dense trajectories, and identifies critical steps for online intervention. These findings suggest that action preferences are useful for tracking agentic misalignment during reasoning. Our code and data are accessible: https://github.com/RebeccaZhang22/intent-as-a-tool.

title: Concepts Whisper: Spectral Anti-Concentration and the Dual Geometry of Transformer Representations
abstract: We find that transformer concept representations systematically anti-concentrate in the spectral tail of the unembedding covariance, encoding word-level concepts in low-variance directions across a 17-model core suite and an expanded set of 22 semantic concept categories, with convergent replications from three independent extraction methods. Residual-stream difference-of-means vectors anti-concentrate in all 17 models (model-level one-sample t-test, p = 3.8e-9), and remain more tail-aligned than norm-matched random directions in 13 of 17; convergent support comes from sparse autoencoder (SAE) features (p = 4.5e-19 across concepts within a model) and linear probes on Llama and Qwen. We identify a dual geometry: activation-space concept directions anti-concentrate while static unembedding-row contrasts concentrate in high-variance directions (p < 10\textasciicircum-4). This investigation arose from testing whether the causal inner product of Park et al. (2024) aids cross-lingual concept transport; a matched-spectrum randomization across 17 models and four language pairs finds no evidence that Whitened Causal Alignment improves over spectral regularization alone (p = 0.95). Split-injection interventions, restricted to steering strengths at which both arms remain interpretable, show the predicted interference asymmetry in four of five models (paired Cohen's d\_z up to 1.19) with no significant reversal inside that regime, and POS-tag probing across eight models shows syntax preferentially encoded in the high-variance subspace in six of eight architectures, with a significant reversal in the Qwen 2.5 family. These results suggest transformers rotate semantic content into spectrally quiet regions during contextualized processing, where, in some architectures, interventions may reduce grammatical disruption relative to high-variance steering.

title: Few-shot Semantic Recovery Attacks on Image Embeddings
abstract: Image embeddings are an essential commodity in modern AI: stored at scale in vector databases, transferred between edge devices and cloud APIs, and traded as paid services. Image embeddings have been implicitly treated as anonymous---an assumption that has not been rigorously tested even as embedding services scale to billions of stored vectors. We show this assumption breaks. We propose Cross-modal Recovery Attack with Few-shot Transfer (CRAFT), a framework that recovers semantic meaning, including free-form captions and sensitive attributes. The attack focuses on the medical domain and facial features, targeting black-box image embeddings without reconstructing a single image in pixels and without any knowledge of the underlying model architecture, training data, or weights. CRAFT combines a public dual-encoder, a linear alignment learned from intercepted image-embedding pairs, and a fine-tuned embedding-to-text decoder; we further strengthen recovery with two augmentative techniques: cross-modal reranking against the attacker's text encoder and chain-of-thought prompting on a diffusion-rendered low-fidelity reconstruction of the leaked embedding. Attacks succeed with as few as a single intercepted pair and transfer across five open-source and proprietary embedders. We disclose a privacy surface that current defenses cannot close. Every setting that preserves downstream utility also leaves the attack effective. Black-box image embeddings, as widely deployed in AI systems today, should not be treated as privacy-preserving artifacts.

title: Beyond Consensus: Perspectivist Modeling and Evaluation of Annotator Disagreement in NLP
abstract: Annotator disagreement is widespread in NLP, particularly for subjective and ambiguous tasks such as toxicity detection and stance analysis. While early approaches treated disagreement as noise to be removed, recent work increasingly models it as a meaningful signal reflecting variation in interpretation and perspective. This survey provides a unified view of disagreement-aware NLP methods. We first present a domain-agnostic taxonomy of the sources of disagreement spanning data, task, and annotator factors. We then synthesize modeling approaches using a common framework defined by prediction targets and pooling structure, highlighting a shift from consensus learning toward explicitly modeling disagreement, and toward capturing structured relationships among annotators. We review evaluation metrics for both predictive performance and annotator behavior, and noting that most fairness evaluations remain descriptive rather than normative. We conclude by identifying open challenges and future directions, including integrating multiple sources of variation, developing disagreement-aware interpretability frameworks, and grappling with the practical tradeoffs of perspectivist modeling.
